body.text: The SR&ED expenditure pool under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act lets taxpayers carrying on business in Canada accumulate allowable current and, after December 15, 2024, capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada. The pool is reduced by government assistance and prior-year investment tax credits, can be deducted in any amount, and a positive balance never expires.

Canada’s research and development (R&D) tax incentive ecosystem—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) programme and complemented by ten provincial and territorial R&D tax credit regimes—has undergone its most consequential legislative expansion in over a decade1. Enacted into law on March 26, 2026, via Royal Assent to Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) following announcements in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) and Federal Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025), the federal reforms apply retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 20241. These statutory amendments double the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual federal cash refund from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000), extend the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time, widen the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000 alongside a new three-year average gross revenue phase-out alternative, and reinstate full deductibility and ITC eligibility for capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs acquired or first becoming payable after December 15, 20241. Furthermore, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an elective Pre-Claim Approval Process that delivers up-front technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and accelerates post-filing expenditure reviews from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days, while Federal Budget 2026 introduced subsequent proposals to expand SR&ED coverage to commercialisation and intellectual property (IP) protection expenses1.

At the sub-national level, major structural realignments have occurred concurrently across Canadian provinces10. In its March 25, 2025 budget, Québec abolished its legacy R&D tax credits and replaced them—for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025—with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d’impôt pour la recherche, l’innovation et la commercialisation, or CRIC), offering a 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of qualified R&D and pre-commercialisation expenditures above an exclusion threshold (at least $50,000) and 20% on excess expenditures regardless of corporate asset size10. British Columbia’s Budget 2026 and Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) made the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit permanent and harmonised it retroactively with federal Bill C-15 by doubling the refundable expenditure limit to $6,000,000, extending refundable eligibility to ECPCs, raising the taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, and restoring capital expenditure eligibility11. Similarly, Saskatchewan doubled its 10% refundable CCPC expenditure threshold from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 202412.

This report provides a comprehensive legal, technical, and financial audit of Canada’s federal, provincial, and territorial R&D tax laws, qualifying expenditure rules, overhead calculation methodologies, compliance procedures, CRA review protocols, judicial precedents from the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal, and non-dilutive grant stacking mechanics as of late 20261.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Programme
1.1 Core Statutory Framework: The Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Programme is Canada’s largest single source of federal support for business-led innovation1. During fiscal year 2024–2025, the programme delivered $4.5 billion in investment tax credits to more than 19,000 claimants across over 22,000 processed claims1. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) reported $4.9 billion in investment tax credits claimed and $4.6 billion allowed, representing a roughly 50% expansion in total credit value since fiscal 20221.

Unlike discretionary grant programmes that operate under fixed budgetary envelopes, the SR&ED programme is a statutory entitlement embedded within the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the “ITA” or the “Act”) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the “Regulations”)18. If a taxpayer’s technical activities and associated expenditures satisfy the statutory definitions and are reported on prescribed forms by the statutory reporting deadline, the Minister of National Revenue is legally obligated to allow the deduction and issue the corresponding tax credit22.
The programme delivers two distinct, sequential tax incentives under the Income Tax Act11:

items: Immediate and Indefinite Income Tax Deduction (Section 37 ITA): Under subsection 37(1) of the Act, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada that are related to a business of the taxpayer26. These pooled expenditures override the general deduction prohibitions in section 18 of the Act and may be deducted in full in the current taxation year to reduce net business income for tax purposes, or carried forward indefinitely in a running pool balance to offset business income in any future taxation year26.

Investment Tax Credit (Sections 127 and 127.1 ITA): Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act, a claimant earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a specified percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of its “SR&ED qualified expenditure pool” at the end of the taxation year5. Depending on the claimant’s legal status, taxable capital or gross revenue, and prior-year taxable income, unused ITCs after offsetting Part I federal income tax payable may be refunded in cash under section 127.1 of the Act, carried back 3 taxation years, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years2.

body.text: 1.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED (Subsection 248(1)) and the “Why” and “How” Eligibility Framework

To qualify for federal SR&ED tax incentives, the technical work performed must satisfy the statutory definition of “scientific research and experimental development” in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act24. The statute defines SR&ED as a “systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis”24 and divides the universe of activities into four eligible categories (paragraphs (a) to (d)) and seven explicit exclusions (paragraphs (e) to (k))31:

items: Basic Research (Paragraph 248(1)(a)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view31. Basic research seeks to expand the foundational scientific knowledge base (for example, investigating the properties of newly discovered elementary particles or characterizing a novel viral mechanism) and is typically conducted in laboratory environments by biotechnology, nanotechnology, advanced materials, or computing enterprises, often in collaboration with universities or research institutes31.

Applied Research (Paragraph 248(1)(b)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view31. For example, while characterizing a newly identified virus constitutes basic research, investigating how to exploit those viral characteristics to formulate an effective vaccine constitutes applied research31.

Experimental Development (Paragraph 248(1)(c)): Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto31. Experimental development is by far the most frequently claimed category in Canadian corporate SR&ED filings31. Crucially, the commercial novelty, uniqueness, or feature enhancement of a product or process does not in itself constitute SR&ED; the work must be undertaken specifically to generate or discover technological knowledge or know-how that resolves an underlying technological uncertainty31.

Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d)): Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories—(i) engineering, (ii) design, (iii) operations research, (iv) mathematical analysis, (v) computer programming, (vi) data collection, (vii) testing, or (viii) psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development (described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c)) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer31. Support work never qualifies as SR&ED on a standalone basis; its eligibility is strictly derivative of, and bounded by, the core (a), (b), or (c) experimental work it directly supports31.

Statutorily Excluded Work (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)): The definition of SR&ED expressly excludes work with respect to: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; or (k) routine data collection31.

body.text: As the CRA emphasises in its administrative guidelines, distinguishing between eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as “data collection” or “testing”) and excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) (“routine testing” or “routine data collection”) turns entirely on purpose31. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically and directly to test a hypothesis and resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty within an SR&ED investigation, it qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph (d); if it is performed to verify commercial compliance, quality assurance, or standard operational performance, it is excluded31.
Evolution of Administrative Guidance: From IC 86-4 and the Five Questions to the “Why” and “How” Requirements

Historically, federal guidance on SR&ED eligibility evolved from Interpretation Bulletin IT-439 (pre-1985) to the May 23, 1985 Budget Papers (which added “experimental development” to exclude routine engineering), and then to Information Circular IC 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development, 1986; revised as IC 86-4R3 in 1994), which articulated three core criteria: scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and scientific and technical content52. In 1998, Justice Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada synthesised IC 86-4R3 and the statutory text of subsection 248(1) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen into a five-criteria test, which the CRA subsequently codified as the “Five Questions” in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published in 2012 and revised in 2015)21.

In August 2021, the CRA archived the 2015 policy and promulgated the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives25. While the Federal Court of Appeal has repeatedly confirmed (in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72) that the common-law Northwest Hydraulic test governs the interpretation of the statutory definition in subsection 248(1), and the 2021 Guidelines did not alter that statutory definition, the CRA now structures its administrative reviews around two overarching pillars—the “Why” Requirement and the “How” Requirement21.

Under the “Why” Requirement (Scientific or Technological Uncertainty and Attempted Advancement), work must be conducted for the purpose of advancing scientific knowledge or achieving a technological advancement31. A technological advancement requires the generation or discovery of conceptual knowledge or know-how that advances the taxpayer’s understanding of technology, rather than merely collecting factual measurements or acquiring publicly available or proprietary knowledge through training, on-the-job learning, or hiring external consultants31. The starting point of any SR&ED project is scientific or technological uncertainty—a situation where it is uncertain whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, because the combined knowledge base of the business’s internal technical staff and publicly accessible scientific/technological sources is insufficient31. Indicators of technological uncertainty include non-applicable existing design methods, specifications that conflict with established standards, interlocking constraints, excessive unknown variables, or operating parameters outside normal ranges31. While purely economic or cost targets do not in themselves constitute technological uncertainty, attempting to meet a stringent cost constraint by altering materials or process architectures can introduce genuine technological uncertainty31. Crucially, whether the project succeeds or fails in achieving its commercial or technical objective is irrelevant to eligibility; failing an experiment and demonstrating that a hypothesised pathway is unviable still generates technological advancement by eliminating uncertainty31.

Under the “How” Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search), the work must be carried out through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, performed or supervised by qualified personnel24. Unlike routine trial-and-error or standard business troubleshooting, a systematic investigation requires four sequential, documented steps25:

items: Formulating a Hypothesis: Generating a specific idea or proposed solution consistent with known scientific/technological facts as a starting point to resolve the identified uncertainty25.

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Rigorously testing the hypothesis through planned physical experiments, prototypes, simulations, or mathematical/engineering analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve iteratively based on test outcomes25.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Analysing the quantitative and qualitative results of the experiments to draw logical conclusions regarding why the hypothesis succeeded or failed24.
Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Maintaining dated records, logs, test data, and artefacts generated as the work progresses to substantiate the hypotheses tested and the conclusions reached25.

body.text: 1.3 The 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms: Bill C-15, Budget 2025, and Budget 2026

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the federal SR&ED programme underwent a multi-stage legislative overhaul that reversed the austerity cuts of the 2012 Federal Budget (which had eliminated capital expenditures and reduced the basic ITC rate from 20% to 15% effective in 2014) and modernised corporate eligibility1. Tax practitioners and auditors must track the exact legislative timeline to avoid applying superseded draft figures:

items: 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) & Draft Legislative Proposals (August 15, 2025): Initially proposed increasing the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000 (which would have yielded a maximum refundable credit of $1,575,000), raising the taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring capital expenditure eligibility for property acquired on or after December 16, 20242.

Federal Budget 2025 (Tabled November 4, 2025 by Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne): Confirmed all structural expansions from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and further increased the annual enhanced expenditure limit from the previously proposed $4,500,000 to $6,000,000, doubling the historical $3,000,000 limit and raising the maximum annual refundable federal ITC to $2,100,000, retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 20242.

Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 — Royal Assent on March 26, 2026): Formally enacted the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 taxable capital and 3-year average gross revenue phase-out formulas, ECPC eligibility for the 35% refundable credit, and the restoration of capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs into the Income Tax Act, effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and for capital property acquired or lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024)1. The Department of Finance estimated that approximately 550 scaling CCPCs immediately benefit from the higher expenditure limit and phase-out thresholds, alongside newly qualifying public scale-ups6.

CRA Administrative Modernisation (Effective April 1, 2026 & May–October 2026 Policy Releases): On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the elective Pre-Claim Approval Process via My Business Account, deployed AI-supported claim risk screening to expedite low-risk filings, and subsequently issued revised Form T661 (May 15, 2026), updated Schedule T2SCH31 (May 22, 2026), updated Schedule T2SCH49 (May 29, 2026), and updated administrative policies for Shared-Use Equipment (May 22, 2026), Total Qualified Expenditures (May 22, 2026), Lease Expenditures (June 8, 2026), Capital Expenditures (June 29, 2026), and Investment Tax Credits (October 7, 2026)1.

Federal Budget 2026 Commercialisation Expansion Proposals: Building on the Bill C-15 reforms, Federal Budget 2026 proposed expanding the SR&ED programme to cover specific commercialisation expenses associated with bringing a new product or process to market—specifically costs to obtain necessary regulatory approvals or certifications, and costs to secure and maintain intellectual property (IP) protection—for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day, backed by $930 million in federal funding over five years and $235 million per year ongoing8.

body.text: 2. Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Phase-Out Mechanics, and Carryovers
2.1 Dual-Tier Credit Rates (35% Enhanced vs. 15% Basic) and Entity Eligibility
The federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit operates on a two-tier rate structure governed by subsections 127(9) and 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act5.

The Basic ITC Rate (15%) is earned on the excess of a claimant’s SR&ED qualified expenditure pool over any provincial super-allowance benefit amounts5. The 15% rate applies to large Canadian public corporations, foreign-controlled corporations, and other corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs; to CCPCs and ECPCs on the portion of their annual qualified SR&ED expenditures that exceeds their available expenditure limit ($6,000,000 or their phased-out limit); to individuals operating sole proprietorships; to beneficiaries of trusts; and to members of a partnership allocated credits under subsection 127(8)1.

The Enhanced ITC Rate (35%)—consisting of the 15% basic rate plus an additional 20% enhancement under subsection 127(10.2)—is available on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation’s annual expenditure limit (maximum $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024)5. Two classes of corporations qualify for the 35% enhanced rate: Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)2.
Under subsection 127(9), to qualify as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC), a corporation must satisfy four cumulative conditions throughout the taxation year2:

items: Be resident in Canada2;
Have a class of shares of its capital stock listed on a designated stock exchange, or have elected or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue to be a public corporation2;
Not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons2; and
Maintain an average annual consolidated gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years of less than $75,000,000 (the upper phase-out boundary)2.

body.text: Additionally, Canadian-resident corporations where all or substantially all (90% or more) of the shares are owned by one or more ECPCs are also eligible to claim the enhanced refundable ITC2. By extending the 35% refundable rate to ECPCs, Parliament removed the steep decline in R&D support that previously penalised Canadian scale-ups when transitioning from a CCPC to a publicly listed corporation4.
Special Statutory Rule for Partnerships (Subsection 127(8))

Under Canadian tax law, a partnership is not a separate taxpayer under the Income Tax Act; rather, income, losses, and credits are computed at the partnership level under subsection 96(1) and allocated to the partners27. Consequently, a partnership cannot directly earn ITCs and cannot earn the 35% enhanced ITC rate, even if its partners are CCPCs41. The SR&ED ITC of a partnership is strictly determined using the 15% basic rate on the partnership’s qualified expenditures and allocated at the end of the partnership’s fiscal period to eligible partners under subsection 127(8)5. Furthermore, under subsections 96(2.4) and 248(1), any partner who is a “specified member” of the partnership—defined as any limited partner or any general partner who was not regularly, continuously, and substantially actively engaged in the activities of the partnership’s business (other than financing) during the year—cannot receive an allocation of SR&ED ITCs41. Under subsection 127(12.1), the SR&ED ITC allocated by the partnership to its partners reduces the partnership’s subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the subsequent taxation year, and because a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance, any remaining pool balance at the end of the partnership’s fiscal year must be deducted in full in computing the partnership’s net income for that year26.
2.2 Mathematical Formulas for the $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Reductions

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit of $6,000,000 is subject to a straight-line reduction (phase-out) once a corporate group’s size exceeds $15,000,000, reaching zero at $75,000,0001. Depending on whether the claimant is a CCPC or an ECPC, the phase-out is calculated using either Prior-Year Taxable Capital Employed in Canada or 3-Year Average Annual Gross Revenue2.
Method A: Prior-Year Taxable Capital Employed in Canada Phase-Out (Default for CCPCs)

Unless a CCPC files a prescribed election to use the gross revenue method, its expenditure limit is determined by the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and all associated corporations for their immediately preceding taxation year2. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit began phasing out at $10,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital and was completely eliminated at $50,000,000 (a reduction of $0.075 for every $1 of taxable capital exceeding $10,000,000)1. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit remains unreduced if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less2. Above $15,000,000, the limit is reduced by $0.10 for every $1 of prior-year taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,0002.

To illustrate, suppose a CCPC (with no associated corporations and a full 365-day taxation year ending December 31, 2025) had $35,000,000 of taxable capital employed in Canada in its 2024 taxation year2. Because its prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 by $20,000,000 ($35,000,000 − $15,000,000), its $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $0.10 × $20,000,000 = $2,000,000, leaving an enhanced expenditure limit of $4,000,0002. If the CCPC incurs $5,000,000 of qualified SR&ED current expenditures in 2025, the first $4,000,000 earns the 35% enhanced ITC ($1,400,000) and the remaining $1,000,000 earns the 15% basic ITC ($150,000)2.
Method B: 3-Year Average Consolidated Gross Revenue Phase-Out (Mandatory for ECPCs, Elective for CCPCs)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) must calculate their expenditure limit phase-out based on their average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years2. CCPCs may also elect on a prescribed form to have their expenditure limit determined under this gross revenue method instead of the taxable capital method—a major advantage for capital-intensive clean-tech, hardware, biotechnology, or manufacturing CCPCs that have raised substantial equity or debt financing (pushing their taxable capital above $15,000,000) while generating limited commercial revenue during their R&D phase2.

Under the gross revenue calculation rules, for a standalone corporation that is not a member of a corporate group preparing consolidated financial statements, gross revenue is the amount reported in its annual financial statements prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) presented to shareholders2. For a corporation that is a member of a corporate group preparing consolidated financial statements, gross revenue is the total amount reflected in the group’s annual consolidated financial statements presented to shareholders at the highest level of consolidation for the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout the entirety of that three-year period, and all members of the corporate group must share access to the single $6,000,000 expenditure limit2. The $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis by $0.10 for every $1 by which the three-year average annual gross revenue (GR) exceeds $15,000,000, and is reduced to nil once GR reaches $75,000,0002:
Proration for Short Taxation Years (Subsection 127(10.5)) and Associated Corporations (Subsection 127(10.3))

If a corporation has a short taxation year (less than 51 weeks), its calculated expenditure limit must be prorated under subsection 127(10.5) by multiplying the limit by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 3655:
Prorated expenditure limit = Expenditure limit × (Number of days in the taxation year ÷ 365)

For instance, as illustrated in the CRA’s SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a corporation has a 184-day taxation year running from July 1 to December 31, its expenditure limit is multiplied by 184 ÷ 365 (for example, $3,000,000 × [184 ÷ 365] = $1,512,328, or under the $6,000,000 limit, $6,000,000 × [184 ÷ 365] = $3,024,658)5. Furthermore, where a CCPC is associated with one or more other CCPCs in a taxation year, the single expenditure limit must be allocated among the associated corporations using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3)7. Specific rules also apply if a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC having a taxation year ending in that same calendar year5.

2.4 Section 37 Deductible Pool Mechanics, ITC Carryovers, and Loss Restriction Events (Subsection 37(6.1))
The Subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

In every taxation year, a claimant’s allowable SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada accumulate in a running pool under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act26. In Part 3 (Section C) of Form T661, the pool available for deduction at the end of the taxation year is calculated by taking the prior-year ending pool balance and applying statutory additions and reductions24.
Under Section 3.1 of the CRA’s Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, the subsection 37(1) pool is increased by six statutory additions26:

items: Allowable current SR&ED expenditures incurred in the year in Canada (paragraph 37(1)(a)), comprising the eligible portion of directly engaged employee salaries or wages, the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, 100% of contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant, eligible third-party payments, and—when the Traditional Method is elected—allowable SR&ED overhead expenditures26;
Allowable capital SR&ED expenditures for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (paragraph 37(1)(b))7;
Repayments made in the year of government or non-government assistance that had previously reduced the pool (paragraph 37(1)(c))26;
Any negative pool balance included in the claimant’s income in the preceding taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v) (added back under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) to reset the opening pool balance to nil)26;
Pool balances transferred to the claimant upon an amalgamation or wind-up26; and
The amount of any federal SR&ED ITC recaptured in the immediately preceding taxation year (or amounts added due to a partnership ITC recapture excess amount)26.

items: Government assistance (including provincial/territorial R&D tax credits and grants) and non-government assistance that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive for SR&ED expenditures included in the pool (paragraph 37(1)(d))26;
Any provincial super-allowance benefit amount for the year or preceding taxation years (paragraph 37(1)(d.1))26;

Federal SR&ED ITCs applied and/or refunded in a preceding taxation year (reported on Line 435 of Form T661)—because the federal ITC deducted from Part I tax or received as a cash refund in Year 1 reduces the Section 37 deductible pool in Year 2 (or is included in business income under paragraph 12(1)(v) in Year 2 if the pool becomes negative), the federal SR&ED ITC is effectively brought into taxable income in the following taxation year24;
Amounts deducted from the pool under subsection 37(1) (or deducted in respect of insolvency under section 61.3) in previous taxation years26; and
Reductions to nil upon a loss restriction event under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1)26.

body.text: A positive balance in the subsection 37(1) pool never expires26. A corporate, individual, or trust claimant may choose to deduct the entire pool balance, any partial amount, or $0 in a given taxation year, carrying forward the undeducted balance indefinitely to shelter taxable business income in future profitable years26.
ITC Carryback (3 Years), Carryforward (20 Years), and Loss Restriction Events

Under subsection 127(5) and the definition of “investment tax credit” in subsection 127(9), any portion of a current-year SR&ED ITC that is not applied to reduce Part I tax payable in the current year and is not refunded in cash under section 127.1 (since refunded ITCs are deemed by subsection 127.1(3) to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable) may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in those prior years (limited to the lesser of the current-year undeducted ITC and the prior year’s Part I tax otherwise payable in excess of ITCs available in that prior year), or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset future Part I tax otherwise payable, after which any unapplied ITC expires2.

When a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust experiences a new majority-interest beneficiary)—a loss restriction event—strict streaming rules apply5. Under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1), the corporation’s subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures accumulated prior to the acquisition of control is reduced to nil, and can only be reinstated and deducted in a subsequent taxation year when the business to which the expenditure related is continued for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent that the corporation’s income for that tax year (before making any Section 37 pool deduction) is from that same business or a similar business26. Similarly, carryforwards of unused ITCs earned before an acquisition of control, and carrybacks of unused ITCs earned after an acquisition of control, are restricted5.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methodologies, and Reinstated Capital Rules
3.1 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, Foreign R&D, and the 180-Day Unpaid Rule

Salaries and wages constitute the largest expenditure category in most Canadian SR&ED claims61. Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, “salary or wages” means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (i.e., T4 employment remuneration), and explicitly excludes the employer’s share of related payroll benefits (such as Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Employment Insurance (EI), or Workers’ Compensation Board (WCB) premiums), stock option benefits, retiring allowances, and extended vacation or sick leave30.
Directly Engaged vs. Non-Directly Engaged Salaries (Proxy vs. Traditional Method)

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, only the portion of salary or wages of employees who are “directly engaged” in the prosecution of SR&ED can be claimed on Form T66120. As defined in the CRA’s SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy and SR&ED Glossary, “directly engaged” means hands-on work determined by the actual tasks performed rather than the employee’s job title43. Directly engaged tasks include preparing and conducting experiments, performing eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, directly supervising technical staff, and technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects (such as assigning technological personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, or evaluating quality of materials used)62. Tasks performed by non-specialised employees (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a machine) also qualify as directly engaged provided they are supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications62. Conversely, salaries relating to administrative or clerical support work that is not directly engaged cannot be claimed under the Proxy Method because those costs are captured by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)20.

When a claimant elects the Traditional Method, in addition to hands-on directly engaged salaries, the claimant may claim (on Line 360 of Form T661 as overhead and other expenditures) the salaries and wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support the prosecution of SR&ED (including clerical and administrative staff whose tasks are directly related and incremental to the SR&ED) as well as the employer’s share of related benefits and retiring allowances for hands-on SR&ED employees20.
Specified Employee Restrictions (5 × YMPE Deduction Cap, 75% / 2.5 × YMPE Proxy Cap, and Form T1174)

A “specified employee” of a claimant is defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who is a “specified shareholder” of the employer—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of a related corporation (including shares owned by persons with whom the employee does not deal at arm’s length)—or who otherwise does not deal at arm’s length with the employer (for example, a spouse, sister, or brother of a specified shareholder)30.
To prevent owner-managers from converting corporate profits into refundable SR&ED tax credits, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose four strict limitations on specified employees30:

items: Complete Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration: Bonuses and any remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages (bonuses and profit-based remuneration are allowed only for non-specified employees)30.

Maximum Allowable SR&ED Salary Cap (5 × YMPE and 75% Maximum): The maximum amount that a claimant can claim as an allowable SR&ED expenditure (Line 305 of Form T661) for the salary or wages of a specified employee is limited to the time directly engaged in SR&ED (up to a maximum of 75%) and cannot exceed 5 times the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE)—as determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan (the first earnings ceiling, not the second YAMPE ceiling)—for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee24.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap (Lesser of 75% of Total Wages or 2.5 × YMPE): Under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations, the maximum amount that a claimant can include in the salary base (Part 5 of Form T661) to calculate the 55% PPA for a specified employee is restricted to the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee’s total salary or wages (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED) for the year, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year; or (b) 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days (B) in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual using the formula 2.5 × YMPE × (B ÷ 365)34.

Associated Corporation Rules (Form T1174 and Shared Caps): If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, no SR&ED expenditure may be claimed for that specified employee unless the associated corporations file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED))—accompanied by a certified copy of the authorizing directors’ resolution (or sole shareholder confirmation)—no later than the corporations’ respective SR&ED reporting deadlines23. Otherwise, the amount is deemed not to be an expenditure on SR&ED30. Both the 5 × YMPE expenditure cap (under s. 37(9.3)) and the 2.5 × YMPE proxy salary base cap (under Regulation 2900(8)) must be shared across all associated corporations23.

body.text: Unpaid Amounts and the 180-Day Rule (Subsection 127(26))

Under subsection 127(26) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA’s SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, if an SR&ED expenditure—including accrued salaries or wages—is incurred in a taxation year but remains unpaid 180 days after the end of that taxation year, the expenditure is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year30. Instead, the unpaid salary must be identified on Line 315 of Form T661 in the year accrued, and is deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (reported on Line 310 of Form T661 in the year of payment)24. Payment made on the 180th day satisfies the time limit30. The best evidence of payment is timely remittance of payroll source deductions (generally within 15 days after the month withheld), supported by T4 slips, employee income reporting, cheques, cash, or journal entries crediting the employee’s account; an ordinary promissory note is treated as a promise to pay at a later date rather than absolute payment unless an explicit agreement establishes it was accepted as absolute payment30. Reasonable vacation or holiday pay and deferred amounts under a salary deferral arrangement (subsection 248(1)) are deemed paid for Section 37 deductibility, though they are excluded from the PPA salary base30.
3.2 Overhead Methodologies: Proxy Method (55% PPA) vs. Traditional Method

Every SR&ED claimant must select in Part 3, Section A of Form T661 between two methods of calculating SR&ED expenditures and accounting for overhead: the Proxy Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162)20.
The Proxy Method and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Subsection 37(10) and Regulation 2900(4))

Most Canadian SR&ED claimants elect the Proxy Method because of its administrative simplicity and notional credit uplift20. Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically identify, track, or allocate overhead and other expenditures for SR&ED on Form T66120. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional amount known as the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 (Line 820) of Form T661 equal to 55% of its eligible SR&ED salary base (subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, which has stood at 55% since 2014, following reductions from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013)20. The salary base consists solely of the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, subject to the specified employee 75% / 2.5 × YMPE cap, and never includes contractor costs24.

Because the PPA is a notional substitute for overhead (covering general-purpose office equipment or furniture, support or clerical staff wages, office supplies, utilities, and other overhead), the PPA is not included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the actual overhead expenses that the PPA represents are deducted by the business as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1) of the Act20. However, under subsection 127(9), the PPA is added directly to the claimant’s qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 502 of Form T661 (subject to the overall cap on the PPA), where it earns the 35% enhanced (or 15% basic) federal ITC and applicable provincial R&D tax credits (such as Ontario’s OITC/ORDTC and BC’s SR&ED credit, though not Québec’s CRIC)20. At the 35% federal rate, the 55% PPA adds a 19.25% (35% × 55%) federal tax credit onto every dollar of eligible non-specified T4 SR&ED salary, bringing the effective federal ITC on T4 labour alone to 54.25% before provincial credits20.
The Traditional Method: Directly Related and Incremental Overhead (Regulation 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3))

Under the Traditional Method, no PPA is calculated20. Instead, the claimant must specifically identify, track, substantiate, and allocate its actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures and report them on Line 360 of Form T66124. These actual overhead expenditures are added both to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and to the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool to earn ITCs20.

As detailed in the CRA’s SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, accounting overhead under Canadian GAAP (indirect costs) does not automatically qualify as SR&ED overhead37. Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Act and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations, an overhead expenditure qualifies under the Traditional Method only if it falls into one of two regulatory categories20:

First, under Paragraph 2900(2)(c) (Expenditures Directly Attributable to the Prosecution of SR&ED), an expenditure (or a reasonable portion thereof) must pass two cumulative statutory tests: the Directly Related Test and the Incremental Test37. Under the Directly Related Test, “direct” means proceeding straight without deviation, interruption, or an intervening step37. As established by the Tax Court of Canada in Ergorecherche et Conseils Inc. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1710) and Quantetics Corporation v. The Queen (2000 DTC 2177), there must be a direct linkage between the expense and (a) specific SR&ED work, (b) SR&ED staff, or (c) machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED37. For example, salaries, employer-paid related benefits, and retiring allowances of hands-on SR&ED staff have a direct linkage to SR&ED work37. By contrast, while the salary of a clerical or administrative employee who performs tasks directly aiding ongoing SR&ED (e.g., non-technological tasks in HR, accounting, or purchasing) can be claimed if directly linked and incremental, that clerical employee’s related benefits, retiring allowance, training, or travel costs are indirectly linked and disallowed37. Under the Incremental Test, the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred37. For example, long-distance telephone charges directly related and incremental to SR&ED qualify, whereas fixed monthly telephone, cell phone, and internet costs are standard non-incremental business expenses and do not qualify37. Allowable Regulation 2900(2)(c) overhead includes the employer’s share of related benefits and retiring allowances for hands-on SR&ED staff; non-SR&ED support contracts (e.g., electricians, welders, mechanics) directly related and incremental to SR&ED; moving expenses to relocate SR&ED employees; travel and lodging in Canada to perform testing at a customer location; SR&ED-related training in Canada; utilities and periodical subscriptions; clinical study volunteer fees; and waste disposal costs incurred while the SR&ED activity is active24.

Second, under Subsection 2900(3) (Provision of Premises, Facilities, or Equipment), the cost of maintenance and upkeep of premises, facilities, or equipment used for SR&ED in Canada is specifically allowed by the Regulations and does not need to satisfy separate “directly related” and “incremental” tests, while other provision expenditures (such as property taxes) qualify if they are directly related to that provision and would not have been incurred if those premises, facilities, or equipment had not existed20.
Software and Cloud Space Costs, and Prescribed Exclusions (Regulation 2902)

With respect to software and cloud space costs, KPMG notes in its analysis of the reinstated SR&ED capital and expenditure rules that fees for software and cloud space used for development may qualify depending on how they are used, while the CRA’s Materials for SR&ED Policy specifies that expenditures of a capital nature such as data or software licences cannot be claimed as materials consumed or transformed because materials must be physical and tangible44. Furthermore, under the CRA’s SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy and Regulation 2902, certain prescribed expenditures are disallowed even if they appear directly related and incremental to SR&ED: (1) fees for preparing SR&ED claims, (2) costs to attend conventions or conferences (even if technical and specific to the SR&ED project), and (3) interest expenses37.

body.text: 3.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and ITC Recapture Rules

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Act (Proxy Method) and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations (Traditional Method), a claimant may claim the cost of materials consumed (Line 320 of Form T661) or materials transformed (Line 325 of Form T661) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada20.

As established in the CRA’s Materials for SR&ED Policy, to constitute “materials for SR&ED”, items must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible thing on which the SR&ED is being performed44. Laboratory supplies (petri dishes, beakers, test tubes, pipettes, vials, flasks), cleaning products, used lubricants, general utilities (electricity, water, natural gas), and computer discs (CDs/DVDs) do not compose the body of the object on which SR&ED is performed and therefore do not qualify as materials for SR&ED (though their cost or a portion thereof may qualify as SR&ED overhead under the Traditional Method)44. Materials may be purchased from either Canadian or foreign suppliers provided they are used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada44.

Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials that are destroyed, absorbed, broken down into small pieces, or rendered virtually valueless (disposed of as waste with no residual or resale value) as a result of the prosecution of SR&ED44. Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials incorporated into a custom product, commercial asset, component part, or experimental production run resulting from experimental development (ED+EP) that were not destroyed or rendered virtually valueless44. As detailed in the CRA’s SR&ED During Production Runs Policy and SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy, when developing a custom product or commercial asset or conducting an experimental production run, the claimant must allocate costs between SR&ED work and non-SR&ED commercial work; no cost of materials is allowed for portions of an asset that do not involve SR&ED or for “excess production” beyond what is required for SR&ED43. Furthermore, the cost of materials (which for self-manufactured inventory includes laid-down costs, direct manufacturing salary, and a reasonable portion of production overhead) can only be claimed in the specific taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED (not when purchased or placed in inventory), and must be paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year to earn an ITC44.
Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Whenever a claimant claims SR&ED ITCs on a property—including materials transformed into a product or asset, property acquired under an SR&ED contract, capital expenditures, or shared-use equipment (SUE)—and subsequently sells/disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use, the ITC Recapture Rules in subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act apply2.

As illustrated in Sections 5.1, 7.1, and 7.2 of the CRA’s Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, the definition of “cost” under subsection 127(32) creates a critical distinction between in-house manufacturing and external purchasing45. For recapture purposes, the cost cannot exceed the amount paid by the claimant to acquire a property from another person, and does not include amounts paid by the claimant to maintain, modify, or transform the property45. Consequently, if a corporation manufactures an SR&ED component or batch of inventory in-house, only the cost of the raw materials purchased originally is subject to ITC recapture upon sale or commercial conversion; there is no recapture on the in-house salaries or overhead incurred to manufacture or transform the part45. Conversely, if the corporation orders that same part from an arm’s-length supplier for 12,000(10,000 manufacturing and development cost plus a $2,000 profit element), the entire $12,000 is the cost of property acquired subject to recapture45. Finally, if a payer contracts an arm’s-length performer to conduct SR&ED and the rights to the resulting intellectual property (IP) rest with the payer from inception under the contract, the payer has not acquired property from the performer and will not face ITC recapture if it subsequently sells or leases the rights to the IP45.
3.4 Subcontractors (Arm’s Length vs. Non-Arm’s Length) and Third-Party Payments
Arm’s-Length SR&ED Contracts Performed on Behalf of the Claimant (Line 340 — 80% ITC Inclusion)

When a claimant contracts an arm’s-length party to perform SR&ED on its behalf under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) of the Act, 100% of the allowable contract expenditure enters the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, while 80% of the contract expenditure qualifies as a qualified SR&ED expenditure for calculating the federal SR&ED ITC under subsection 127(9)20.
To claim an arm’s-length SR&ED contract on Line 340 of Form T661, three statutory conditions must be satisfied35:

items: Work Performed Inside Canada: The claimant must show that the SR&ED work performed on its behalf was carried on in Canada by the ultimate performer and was related to a business of the claimant35.

Taxable Supplier Requirement: Under subsection 127(9), the contract amount must be paid or payable to a “taxable supplier”35. If an SR&ED contract expenditure is paid or payable to a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier, it is excluded from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes42.

Nature of the Work (Core SR&ED vs. Support Work Only): As set out in the CRA’s Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, an arm’s-length performer contracted to perform basic research, applied research, or experimental development (along with support work) can claim its own SR&ED expenditures, but must reduce its qualified expenditures for ITC purposes by the “contract payment” received or receivable under subsection 127(18) to avoid duplication of the ITC33. If a payer contracts out only paragraph 248(1)(d) support work to an arm’s-length party, the payer can claim the contract expenditure provided the work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of core SR&ED performed by or on behalf of the payer, whereas the arm’s-length performer cannot claim SR&ED because support work on its own does not meet the definition of SR&ED35.

body.text: Non-Arm’s Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts and Form T1146 Transfers (Line 345)

Where a claimant (payer) enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm’s length (NAL) party under section 251 of the Act, the payer’s contract expenditures (reported on Line 345 of Form T661) are allowable SR&ED expenditures for the payer’s subsection 37(1) deductible pool, but are excluded (0%) from the payer’s qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under paragraph (f) of the definition of “qualified expenditure” in subsection 127(9)24. Conversely, the amount received or receivable by the NAL performer is not considered a “contract payment” and does not reduce the NAL performer’s qualified expenditures; thus, the NAL performer claims its own SR&ED expenditures and ITCs35. Under anti-avoidance rules, a claimant cannot circumvent NAL rules by placing an arm’s-length intermediary between the payer and a NAL performer35.

However, under subsection 127(13) of the Act, the NAL performer and NAL payer may jointly file prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm’s Length), allowing the NAL performer to transfer all or a portion of its qualified SR&ED expenditures in the year to the payer, capped at the lesser of the performer’s qualified expenditures for the year and the contract amount (reported on Line 540 by the performer)7. Because a partnership is not a “taxpayer”, partnerships cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures under subsection 127(13)41. Additionally, when purchasing non-SR&ED goods or services from a NAL supplier, the amount eligible for an ITC is restricted under subsection 127(11.6) to the adjusted service cost or adjusted selling cost to the NAL supplier (reported on Lines 542 and 543 of Form T661)42.
Third-Party Payments (Line 370 and Form T1263) vs. Subcontracts

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) of the Act, a claimant may make Third-Party Payments (reported on Line 370 of Form T661 and Form T1263, Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) to approved associations, approved universities, colleges, research institutes, granting councils, resident corporations, or tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED carried out in Canada related to a business of the claimant23. Like arm’s-length contracts, 80% of a third-party payment qualifies for the federal ITC20. However, third-party payments differ from SR&ED contracts in three fundamental ways: (1) under a third-party payment, the performer controls the SR&ED work and rights are non-exclusive (though the claimant must be entitled to exploit the results), whereas under an SR&ED contract the payer controls the work and typically holds exclusive rights; (2) third-party payments are claimed on a cash basis when paid, whereas SR&ED contracts are claimed on an accrual basis as work is performed; and (3) agricultural producers making check-off contributions to approved agricultural organisations claim their ITCs directly on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) without filing Form T66124.
3.5 Reinstated Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

One of the most impactful pillars of Bill C-15 (enacted March 26, 2026) is the full restoration of SR&ED tax incentives for capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs acquired or first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, reversing the exclusion that applied from 2014 through December 15, 20241.
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Line 390, and Part 6B of Form T661)

As codified in the CRA’s SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), an expenditure incurred to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024 qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 (with the 10 most expensive properties per project listed on Line 262 and the 20 most expensive properties overall detailed in Part 6B, Boxes 780, 782, and 786)7. The expenditure must result in the claimant owning (or holding a leasehold interest in) property that would otherwise qualify for Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) under paragraph 20(1)(a) and subsection 13(21) of the Act27. Non-depreciable property (such as land, inventory, or goodwill) and buildings (or leasehold interests in buildings) are strictly excluded under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e)7.

At the time the property is acquired and becomes available for use (subsection 37(1.2)), the claimant must intend either to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA = 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (meaning anticipated non-SR&ED use does not exceed 10%), or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada2. Under paragraph 37(1)(b), the full capital acquisition cost (including purchase price, installation, customs and excise duties, and transportation) may be deducted in the year via the subsection 37(1) pool; any amount deducted is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed to the claimant, and the property must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (CCA)7.

Critically, while both new and used depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA test qualify for the immediate income deduction on Line 390, only new property (property that has not been used, or acquired for use or lease, for any purpose whatsoever by any previous owner) qualifies for the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit; used equipment (including regular demonstration equipment) must be subtracted on Line 532 of Form T661 and earns 0% ITC2. Under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) is excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures, whereas under the Traditional Method, GPOEF meeting the 90% ASA test qualifies7. For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earning the enhanced 35% ITC on new SR&ED capital property, the resulting ITC is 40% refundable in cash (compared to 100% refundability on current expenditures)2.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Subsection 127(9), Line 504, and Part 6C of Form T661)

When a company acquires new depreciable property after December 15, 2024 that is used for both SR&ED and commercial operations—such that it does not meet the 90% ASA criterion for SR&ED capital expenditures—the property may still earn SR&ED ITCs as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under the CRA’s SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026)7. To qualify, the property must be new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, must not be GPOEF, and must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (which excludes property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED over its useful life, or intended for the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing plant, facility, or line)36.

Unlike the 90% ASA capital test (which evaluates intended use over expected useful life), SUE qualification relies on actual usage during operating time across two defined statutory periods, reported on Line 504 and in Part 6C (Boxes 788–796) of Form T6617:

items: First-Term SUE (Box 794 = “1”): Evaluated over the “first period”, which begins when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time36. If actual operating time for SR&ED in Canada during this first period is primarily (more than 50%) of total operating time, 25% (1/4) of the capital cost of the equipment is deemed to be a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes on Line 5047.

Second-Term SUE (Box 794 = “2”): Evaluated over the “second period”, which begins when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time36. Provided the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE and continues to be used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada over the second period, an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC on Line 5047.

body.text: The capital cost of SUE does not enter the subsection 37(1) SR&ED deductible pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the equipment under regular CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any SUE ITC applied against tax payable or refunded reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the subsequent taxation year7.
3. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Incurred After December 15, 2024)

As set out in the CRA’s SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease expenditures incurred (first becoming payable) after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada are once again allowable current SR&ED expenditures2. Under the Traditional Method, when leased equipment (including GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time in the taxation year for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed as a lease expenditure; if leased equipment (or leased land) is used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED, the claimant can claim the proportional percentage of the lease cost on Line 360 as an overhead and other expenditure, provided it is directly attributable (directly related and incremental) to the SR&ED7.

Under the Proxy Method, if leased equipment (excluding GPOEF and land) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time in the full taxation year for SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), 100% of the lease cost is claimed; if leased equipment is used more than 50% (“primarily”) but less than 90% of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), exactly 50% of the lease cost is claimed; and if leased equipment is used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED, 0% can be claimed38. Under the Proxy Method, lease costs for GPOEF and land are completely excluded38. Under both methods, lease costs for the use or right to use a building (rent) are excluded under subparagraph 37(8)(d)(ii) / 37(8)(e)(i), except for prescribed special-purpose buildings approved by the Department of Finance under Regulation 290320.
4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics
4.1 Mechanics of the Federal-Provincial “Assistance Grind”

In Canada, nine provinces (British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland and Labrador) and one territory (Yukon) offer dedicated R&D tax credits or grants that stack on top of the federal SR&ED ITC, while three jurisdictions (Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut) do not offer a territorial/provincial R&D credit3. Except for Québec (administered by Revenu Québec on the provincial corporate return) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration on the AT1 return), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) via schedules attached to the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return75.

Because provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (and Alberta’s IEG) constitute “government assistance” as defined in subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, they reduce (“grind”) both the federal subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the federal subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool in the year they are earned33. Therefore, a tax auditor or preparer must always calculate the provincial R&D credit first, subtract that provincial credit on Line 429 (Part 3) and Line 513 (Part 4) of Form T661, and then multiply the net federal qualified expenditure pool by the 35% (or 15%) federal ITC rate12. A corporation may legally waive or renounce a provincial R&D tax credit by its income tax return filing-due date if it wishes to avoid reducing its federal SR&ED expenditure pools16.
4.2 Comprehensive Breakdown of Provincial and Territorial Regimes
1. Québec: The New CRIC Regime (Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T)

In the 2025–2026 Québec Budget tabled on March 25, 2025 (and maintained unchanged in the March 18, 2026 Québec Budget), the Gouvernement du Québec enacted a comprehensive overhaul of provincial R&D taxation10. Effective for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec replaced eight previously available tax measures—specifically eliminating the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers (which previously paid a 14% basic rate and up to 30% for SMEs), the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or research consortium, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for technological adaptation services, the industrial design component of the design tax credits (while retaining the fashion design component), and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts10.

In their place, Québec instituted a single, unified, 100% refundable tax credit: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d’impôt pour la recherche, l’innovation et la commercialisation), claimed by filing Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T with the Québec corporate income tax return10. Unlike the former Québec R&D wage credit, the CRIC rate is not based on the asset size of the corporation; all eligible corporations with an establishment in Québec earn 30% fully refundable on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% fully refundable on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 limit10. The annual exclusion threshold is equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec personal income tax Basic Personal Amount ($18,571 in 2025; $18,952 in 2026) for each eligible employee, adjusted to reflect the proportion of time spent by the employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation activities10.

Crucially, the CRIC expands eligibility beyond basic research, applied research, and experimental development to cover pre-commercialisation activities undertaken in Québec as a continuation of R&D carried out in Québec10. Eligible pre-commercialisation activities include (a) tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining initial approvals or certifications needed to market an innovation (including quality control activities directly related to implementing a quality control system required for initial certification), and (b) product design, including form and aesthetic development, functional improvements, and selection of materials10. Qualified CRIC expenditures include 100% of eligible employee salaries and wages in Québec, 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for contracts carried out in Québec, 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity, and 100% of property acquisition costs (capital equipment) used for eligible activities in Québec (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings; cannot be combined with another Québec tax credit such as the C3i credit on the same expense)10.

Québec also maintains the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DICI / DCI), which provides a reduced 2% provincial corporate tax rate (lowering the combined federal-provincial corporate tax rate to 17% from 26.5%) on income from commercialising qualified IP developed in Québec; for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the Québec nexus ratio uses CRIC R&D expenditures (excluding pre-commercialisation expenditures and without subtracting the CRIC exclusion threshold)10. Additionally, Québec’s Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE / CDAEIA) supports IT corporations employing at least six eligible employees meeting specific IT and software gross revenue criteria above the per-employee basic personal amount threshold ($18,571 in 2025), with credit rates reduced by half starting in 2026 where at least 50% of gross revenue derives from services provided to related entities for applications used exclusively outside Québec60.
2. Ontario: OITC (Schedule 566), ORDTC (Schedule 508), and OBRITC (Schedule 568)

Ontario operates three corporate R&D tax credits governed by the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and administered by the CRA16. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566, entered on Line 456 of Schedule 5) provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit (10% for tax years ending before June 1, 2016) to qualifying corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (maximum annual credit of $240,000), shared among associated corporations16. While the federal expenditure limit increased to $6,000,000, Ontario’s OITC limit remains at $3,000,00061. The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit phases out based on two prior-year associated-group tests that compound when both apply: it begins phasing out when prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 (reaching zero at $800,000) and when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $25,000,000 (reaching zero at $50,000,000)68. For example, if a group has $700,000 of prior-year taxable income (leaving $1,000,000, or 1/3, of the limit) and $30,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital (leaving 80% of the limit), the reductions multiply together ($1,000,000 × 80% = $800,000 expenditure limit, for a maximum OITC of $64,000)78. A corporation may waive the OITC in whole or in part under subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario)68.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508, entered on Line 416 of Schedule 5) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) under sections 38 to 44 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment, with no expenditure limit16. Unused ORDTCs carry back 3 years and carry forward 20 years, and may be waived under subsection 43(1)16. Crucially, when a CCPC claims both the 8% OITC and the 3.5% ORDTC, the OITC itself is government assistance for ORDTC purposes and reduces the expenditure base on which the 3.5% ORDTC is calculated (resulting in a combined Ontario credit rate of 8% + [3.5% × 92%] = 11.22%, both of which then reduce the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure base)78.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedule 568 and Schedule 569, entered on Line 458 / Line 470 of Schedule 5) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute in Ontario (universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, or Ontario Centres of Excellence), subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap (maximum annual credit of $4,000,000)16.
3. British Columbia: BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666 — Bill 2, 2026 Reforms)

Governed by Part 6 (sections 97 to 102.6) of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) and amended by Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit provides a 10% credit on SR&ED qualified BC expenditures incurred by corporations with a permanent establishment in British Columbia (individuals are not eligible)11. In Budget 2026, British Columbia made the BC SR&ED Tax Credit permanent and adopted the federal Bill C-15 enhancements for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024: (1) doubling the refundable expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (for a maximum annual refundable BC credit of $600,000); (2) expanding the 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs; (3) raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000; and (4) restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures as BC qualified expenditures11. Qualifying expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 refundable limit for CCPCs/ECPCs, and all qualified BC expenditures for other corporations (including active corporate partners of a partnership), earn a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward; renunciation permitted under subsection 100(1))11. The credit is claimed by filing Form T666 with the T2 return (Line 674 of Schedule 5 for the refundable credit; Line 659 for the non-refundable credit; Line 241 for recapture if BC SR&ED property is disposed of or converted to commercial use within 10 years) no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year11.
4. Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (AT1 Schedule 29 / Form AT29)

Effective January 1, 2021, Alberta replaced its former provincial SR&ED tax credit with the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), a refundable grant delivered through the Alberta corporate income tax system76. The IEG provides qualified corporations that have a permanent establishment in Alberta with an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures (matching federal SR&ED rules) up to the corporation’s base spending level (defined as the corporation’s average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years), plus an enhanced 20% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the two-year average base spending level, up to a maximum annual expenditure cap of $4,000,00074. The grant phases out incrementally between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of taxable capital, with corporations at or above $50,000,000 ineligible77. It is claimed by filing Schedule 29 (Form AT29) with the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1) within 15 months after the corporation’s filing-due date75.
5. Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

In Saskatchewan, under section 63.4 of the Saskatchewan Income Tax Act, 2000, corporations with a Saskatchewan permanent establishment earn a 10% tax credit on eligible Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures (Schedule 403)12. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Saskatchewan doubled the refundable expenditure threshold for CCPCs from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 per year (yielding up to $200,000 in refundable credits entered on Line 645 of Schedule 5)12. Expenditures above $2,000,000 for CCPCs, and all expenditures for non-CCPCs, earn a 10% non-refundable credit (entered on Line 631 of Schedule 5; 3-year carryback and 10-year carryforward; renunciation permitted under subsection 63.4(13)), subject to a combined total annual credit cap of $1,000,000 per corporation (reached at $10,000,000 of expenditures)12.

In Manitoba, under section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba), corporations with a Manitoba permanent establishment earn a 15% tax credit (Schedule 380, no expenditure cap) on eligible Manitoba R&D expenditures, which include current expenditures, capital expenditures for depreciable property (excluding buildings), and first-term and second-term shared-use equipment16. The 15% credit is 100% refundable if the R&D is carried on in Manitoba under an eligible contract with a qualifying research institute; for in-house R&D, 50% is refundable (7.5% effective rate, entered on Line 613 of Schedule 5) and 50% is non-refundable (7.5% effective rate, entered on Line 606 of Schedule 5, with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward; renunciation permitted under subsection 7.3(7)), and expenditures must be identified within 12 months after the T2 filing-due date16.

Across Atlantic Canada and the North, Nova Scotia (section 41 of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia), Schedule 340, Line 566 of Schedule 5, recapture on Line 221, 18-month filing deadline, renunciation within 6 months under s. 41(7)), New Brunswick (section 59 of the New Brunswick Income Tax Act, Schedule 360, Line 597 of Schedule 5, recapture on Line 573), and Newfoundland and Labrador (section 42 of the Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador), Schedule 301 Line 520 for corporations and Form T1129 for individuals, 12-month post-due-date deadline, with eligible expenditures not reduced by non-GST/HST government assistance) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no expenditure cap16. Finally, Yukon (Schedule 442) provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to corporations and resident individuals, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University16.
