body.text: 4.4 Worked Stacking Calculations: Combined Federal + Provincial Recovery
Case 1: Ontario CCPC Claiming OITC + ORDTC + Federal SR&ED (Proxy Method)

Consider an Ontario CCPC in its 2026 taxation year (with prior-year taxable income of $300,000, below the $500,000 OITC threshold, and prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of $5,000,000, below both the $15,000,000 federal and $25,000,000 Ontario thresholds) that incurs $1,000,000 in Ontario SR&ED qualified current expenditures (salaries, the 55% prescribed proxy amount, materials, and 80% of an arm’s-length Ontario contract)78:

items: Calculate Ontario OITC (8% on Schedule 566): Applying the 8% refundable OITC rate to the $1,000,000 Ontario qualified pool yields $80,000 in refundable cash78.

Calculate Ontario ORDTC (3.5% on Schedule 508, Reduced by OITC): Because the OITC reduces the ORDTC expenditure base, the ORDTC base is $1,000,000 − $80,000 = $920,00078. Multiplying $920,000 by 3.5% yields $32,200 in non-refundable Ontario tax credits (giving combined Ontario credits of $112,200, or 11.22% of the qualified pool)78.

Calculate Federal SR&ED ITC (35% on Schedule T2SCH31, Reduced by OITC and ORDTC): Subtracting both the $80,000 OITC and the $32,200 ORDTC from the $1,000,000 pool leaves a federal qualified expenditure base of $887,80078. Multiplying $887,800 by the 35% enhanced rate yields $310,730 in refundable federal ITC78.

Total Combined Recovery: Summing $80,000 (OITC) + $32,200 (ORDTC) + $310,730 (Federal ITC) produces $422,930 (42.29% of the $1,000,000 qualified expenditure pool, of which $390,730 is refunded in cash and $32,200 offsets Ontario corporate income tax)78. If the CCPC has no Ontario income tax payable and waives the $32,200 non-refundable ORDTC under subsection 43(1), its federal qualified base remains $920,000, generating a 35% federal refund of $322,000 and a total 100%-cash recovery of $402,000 ($80,000 + $322,000)16.

Consider a Montréal software CCPC in its 2026 taxation year employing four developers in Québec who spend 60% of their time on eligible SR&ED ($240,000 in eligible SR&ED salaries), plus $30,000 paid to an arm’s-length Québec subcontractor (total actual cash R&D spending = $270,000)60:

items: Calculate Québec CRIC Base and Exclusion Threshold (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T): The CRIC qualified expenditure base equals $240,000 (salaries) + (50% × $30,000 subcontractor) = $255,00014. Comparing the $50,000 minimum threshold against 4 employees × ($18,952 Québec 2026 BPA × 60% SR&ED time) = $45,485, the applicable exclusion threshold is the greater amount of $50,00014.
Calculate Refundable Québec CRIC (30% Rate): Subtracting the $50,000 exclusion threshold from the $255,000 base leaves $205,000; multiplying by 30% yields $61,500 in refundable Québec CRIC60.

Calculate Federal SR&ED Qualified Expenditures and 35% ITC: Gross federal qualified expenditures before assistance equal $240,000 (salaries) + $132,000 (55% PPA on $240,000 salaries) + $24,000 (80% of the $30,000 contract) = $396,00060. Subtracting the expected $61,500 Québec CRIC leaves $334,500 in net federal qualified expenditures60. Multiplying $334,500 by the 35% enhanced rate yields $117,075 in refundable federal ITC60.
Total Combined Cash Recovery: Together, the two credits return $178,575 ($61,500 CRIC + $117,075 federal ITC) in cash on $270,000 of actual cash R&D spending—a 66.14% cash recovery rate60.

5.1 Institutional Governance

The administration of R&D tax incentives in Canada is divided among specialised federal and provincial authorities. The Department of Finance Canada is responsible for federal tax policy, drafting statutory amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations, and approving prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 29036. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the federal SR&ED programme as well as the harmonised provincial and territorial R&D tax credits for British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon60. Within the CRA, the SR&ED Directorate operates through Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs) staffed by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) (who evaluate whether claimed work meets the scientific and technological eligibility criteria) and Financial Reviewers (FRs) (who audit allowable and qualified expenditures)9. In Québec, Revenu Québec and the Ministère des Finances du Québec administer the CRIC, DICI, and CDAE credits14, while in Alberta, Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) administers the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) on the AT1 return75.
5.2 Complete Architecture of Form T661 (Parts 1 to 10) and Prescribed Schedules

To claim federal SR&ED tax incentives, a taxpayer must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15, 2026 to incorporate the Bill C-15 capital, SUE, and lease provisions) alongside the applicable ITC schedule (Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations or Form T2038(IND) for individuals and trusts)7. Claimants using commercial tax preparation software must submit Form T661 electronically and must not submit duplicate paper copies23.

The 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline is an absolute statutory bar23. Under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12) of the Income Tax Act, if a taxpayer fails to file the prescribed forms (both Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information in respect of an expenditure on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline, no amount in respect of the expenditure may be deducted under Section 37, the expenditure is legally deemed not to be an expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED, and the claimant cannot earn any ITC on the expenditure23. The CRA will not allow any additional time after the reporting deadline to remedy deficiencies, and a letter expressing an “intent to file” does not meet the statutory filing requirement23. To avoid forfeiting credits due to a technical omission, the CRA advises submitting the SR&ED claim with the tax return, or at least 90 calendar days before the 18-month reporting deadline so the CRA has time to conduct an initial review and advise the claimant of any missing information before the deadline expires23. Note that Part 9 claim preparer information and the deduction of amounts already identified on time in the subsection 37(1) pool are not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline23.
5.4 Claim Preparer Penalties (Subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3)) and Gross Negligence Penalties (Subsection 163(2))
1. Claim Preparer Information and the $1,000 Shared Penalty (Subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3))

Under subsection 162(5.3) of the Income Tax Act, a “claim preparer” is defined as any person or partnership who agrees to accept consideration to prepare, or assist in preparing, an SR&ED form, expressly excluding an employee who does so in the course of their duties of employment23. Pursuant to paragraph 37(11)(b), Part 9 of Form T661 requires complete disclosure of every claim preparer and their billing arrangement23.

Under subsection 162(5.1), if prescribed information regarding a claim preparer and billing arrangement in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed23. Crucially, both the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable for this $1,000 penalty23. Under subsection 162(5.2), a claim preparer has a statutory due diligence defence if they exercised the degree of care, diligence, and skill that a reasonably prudent person would have exercised in comparable circumstances39. An omission or error in Part 9 triggers the $1,000 penalty but does not disallow the underlying SR&ED claim23.
2. Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2))

As detailed in the CRA’s Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, formerly Application Policy SR&ED 96-05), if a person knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim, the CRA may apply a civil penalty under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act7. Under subsection 163(3), the burden of proof rests on the CRA to show on a balance of probabilities (“more likely than not”) that the false statement or omission resulted from knowing misconduct or gross negligence rather than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act29.

The CRA considers applying the gross negligence penalty where a claimant participates in overstating amounts, claims a project where clear evidence shows the claimant knew it involved no SR&ED, describes SR&ED activities that did not take place while claiming normal business expenses, or continues to claim ineligible, miscalculated, or unsubstantiated amounts after being advised in writing by the CRA that they do not qualify (where not under objection or appeal)29.
When the CRA meets its burden of proof, the penalty under subsection 163(2) is equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of29:

items: Paragraph 163(2)(a) — Understated Part I Tax Payable: The understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission resulting from (i) an understatement of income (which occurs if a disallowed SR&ED expenditure is not a valid ordinary business expense, such as a personal expenditure or false invoice; if the disallowed SR&ED expenditure is still a valid business expense, income is not understated), or (ii) the deduction of an overstated SR&ED ITC from Part I tax payable (in the current year, or in any carryback/carryforward year, with overstated amounts deemed deducted first)29. Under subsection 163(2.1), if a claimant reports a net loss, taxable income is deemed not to be less than zero so the penalty applies to the theoretical Part I tax payable attributable to the understatement of income29.

Paragraph 163(2)(d) — Refund of Overstated Refundable ITC: 50% of the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the claimant29. Notably, per Section 4.3 of the CRA policy, when the gross negligence penalty applies to the refund of a refundable ITC, the CRA calculates the penalty on the entire overstated refund regardless of what caused the overstatement29.

body.text: To illustrate (from Section 5.2 of the CRA policy), suppose a claimant using the Proxy Method knowingly overstates its directly engaged SR&ED salaries by $200,000 (which were valid non-SR&ED business expenses) and also overstates materials consumed by $20,000 due to a simple oversight29. Because the disallowed expenditures are valid business expenses, there is $0 understatement of income, and the $20,000 material error is not penalised because it was a simple oversight29. However, the $200,000 salary overstatement inflates the 55% PPA by $110,000 (55% × $200,000), creating a total overstated base of $310,000 ($200,000 + $110,000)29. At the 35% enhanced ITC rate, the overstated ITC deducted against Part I tax is 35% × $310,000 = $108,500, resulting in a subsection 163(2) gross negligence penalty of 50% × $108,500 = $54,25029.
6. CRA Audit and Review Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, and Landmark Jurisprudence
6.1 Inside the CRA SR&ED Review Process and the 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Programme

In the most recent reporting year, the CRA accepted 90% of SR&ED claims as filed, accepted a further 6% after modifications, and denied only 4%1. When a claim is accepted as filed without a review, the CRA’s target processing time is 60 calendar days22. When a refundable SR&ED claim is selected for a technical and/or financial review (via risk assessment or random sampling), the CRA’s service standard is 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (which the CRA aims to meet 90% of the time; non-refundable claims have no service standard)9.
Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process allowing eligible businesses to find out whether their planned R&D projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives before starting work or incurring costs1. Businesses apply online via My Business Account (covering up to three projects, valid for up to three years), and the CRA provides a formal eligibility determination within eight (8) weeks7. While the claimant must still submit Form T661 with its tax return, when a claim consists of pre-claim approved projects that have not differed significantly from what was initially approved and requires only an expenditure verification review, the CRA’s review processing service standard is cut in half—from 180 calendar days down to 90 calendar days1.
The Three-Step CRA Review Lifecycle and Dispute Resolution Hierarchy

Once an SR&ED claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn, and the Part 10 certification on Form T661 cannot be revoked9. Reviews are conducted by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager, RTM) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager, FRM), primarily via virtual videoconferencing and digital document sharing (with on-site visits approved on an exceptional, case-by-case basis) across three steps9:

items: Step 1 — Start of the Review: Initial telephone contact by a reviewer to provide RTA/FR contact information, confirm language preference, outline the projects and issues under review, discuss required contemporaneous documentation, and schedule the review meeting9.

Step 2 — Review Meeting & Information Requests: Interviews with key technical and financial personnel, a virtual or on-site tour of the premises, examination of supporting technical evidence and financial ledgers, a summary of findings and outstanding items, and deadlines for additional information requests9.

Step 3 — End of the Review & Proposal Package: If adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a Proposal Package containing the RTA’s SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a proposal letter summarising proposed adjustments to expenditures and ITCs (and any proposed monetary penalty), and financial details9. The claimant generally has 30 calendar days from the proposal letter date to accept the findings or submit written representations9.

body.text: Under the CRA’s Guidelines for resolving claimants’ SR&ED concerns, disputes follow a three-step administrative escalation pathway: (1) speak directly with the assigned RTA and/or FR; (2) escalate to the reviewer’s manager (the Research and Technology Manager or Financial Review Manager); and (3) request an Administrative Review after receiving the Proposal Package if concerns remain unresolved9. Following a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection and, if necessary, appeal to the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal9.
6.2 Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence (Tax Court of Canada & Federal Court of Appeal)
Because subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act defines SR&ED in concise statutory terms, Canadian jurisprudence plays a central role in governing audits and appeals54.

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen ([1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC)), Judge Donald Bowman established the foundational five-criteria approach (subsequently endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, (1998) 99 DTC 5087, 235 N.R. 258, and summarised as five questions by the FCA in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393) to determine whether an activity constitutes SR&ED21:

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? (“Routine engineering” describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field28.)
Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?93
Scientific Method: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?91
Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement?50
Contemporaneous Records: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept, as the work progressed?50

body.text: In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 FCA 355) and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016 FCA 152, aff’g 2015 TCC 186), the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the governing judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1)21. In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6), the Tax Court upheld the denial of SR&ED claims for a motorized hydraulic theatre fire-curtain system, finding that the issues were resolved by routine engineering, the team lacked qualified engineering personnel, no proper hypotheses (defined at para 26 as “a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial”) were formulated, and the tests lacked precise measurements (such as exact weights and descent durations), while noting that contemporaneous documentation, though highly beneficial, is not an absolute statutory bar if other credible evidence proves SR&ED occurred92.

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72, aff’g 2020 TCC 47), the Federal Court of Appeal rejected arguments that the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion (“scientific method”) went beyond the text of subsection 248(1) (and, in National R&D, that it had been removed by the CRA’s August 2021 Guidelines on the eligibility of work)21. Furthermore, in National R&D, the FCA upheld the exclusion of the taxpayer’s expert witness report because the expert failed to remain independent and impartial and attempted to establish unproven facts “through the back door”54.

Conversely, in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC) and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 159), the Tax Court of Canada ruled in favour of food-and-beverage claimants28. In Manning Canning Kitchens (involving microbial stability experiments for a room-temperature vinegar-based beverage called “Chrisoda”), Justice Bodie established two vital principles for SR&ED claimants: (1) scientific or technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution or preservative exists, provided it has never been used in the specific context; and (2) contemporaneous documentation does not need to be designed for an outsider unfamiliar with the field to replicate results, so long as it keeps track of the hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained as the work progressed94.

body.text: 7. Direct Government Innovation Grants and Strategic Stacking with SR&ED
7.1 Major Federal Innovation Grant and Contribution Programmes

Beyond the entitlement-based SR&ED tax credit regime, the Government of Canada operates discretionary, pre-approval grant and contribution programmes that provide upfront cash flow during R&D execution90.

The National Research Council of Canada — Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) provides non-dilutive financial assistance and advisory services from Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) to incorporated, for-profit businesses operating in Canada with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent employees that plan to develop and commercialise innovative, technology-driven new or improved products, services, or processes in Canada (sole proprietorships, partnerships, cooperatives, ULCs, and LLCs are ineligible)90. NRC IRAP reimburses up to 80% of internal R&D technical salaries and up to 50% of eligible subcontractor fees for approved projects (with project contributions ranging up to $10,000,000, set case by case by the assigned ITA prior to project start)90. Federal Budget 2026 also provided $298 million ($65M, $107M, and $126M across three fiscal years) for the NRC IRAP Clean Technology renewal8.

For larger capital and scale-up investments, the Strategic Response Fund (initially launched in 2017 as the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) under Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, ISED) provides substantial contributions (typically minimum $10,000,000 contributions in mixed non-repayable and repayable formats) for large-scale innovation and industrial projects4. Additionally, the Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative (RAII) provides interest-free, repayable contributions of $250,000 to $5,000,000 covering up to 50% of eligible project costs for businesses adopting or commercialising AI technologies (repayable starting one year after project completion)90, Mitacs co-funds academic-industrial research internships82, and Federal Budget 2026 initiated policy modernisations across Canada’s three federal granting councils (NSERC, SSHRC, and CIHR) alongside Patent Act ownership registration amendments at the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO)8.
7.2 Legal and Accounting Rules for Government Assistance, Forgivable Loans, and Repayments

As codified in the CRA’s Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, or investment allowance received from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including a Crown corporation, foreign government, or indirectly via a government-funded non-profit entity) in respect of SR&ED constitutes “government assistance” under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act (while inducements or reimbursements from private entities constitute “non-government assistance” under paragraph 12(1)(x) and subsection 127(9))33.
Tax auditors and corporate controllers must enforce five statutory rules when accounting for grants alongside SR&ED33:

items: Accrual Recognition at the Filing-Due Date: Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), assistance reduces both the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool to the extent that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive the assistance on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year33.

Project-by-Project Application Floor at Nil: The assistance reduction is applied strictly on a project-by-project basis33. Assistance received for one project cannot reduce the SR&ED expenditures of another project; it can only reduce the expenditures of the specific project to nil ($0), with any excess assistance included in income for the taxation year33. (Note: For Shared-Use Equipment, as shown in Section 3.5.1 of the CRA’s Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, if assistance exceeds the 25% First-Term SUE qualified expenditure in Year 1, the unapplied assistance balance carries forward to reduce the 25% Second-Term SUE qualified expenditure in Year 236.)

Forgivable Loans and Conditionally Repayable Contributions: Under the Income Tax Act, loans lacking firm terms of repayment—or where repayment is conditional upon profits or revenues, or characterised as royalties—are treated as forgivable loans (government assistance) rather than ordinary business loans, reducing the SR&ED expenditure pool immediately33.

Repayment of Government Assistance (Non-Refundable ITC Rule): When a claimant repays government or non-government assistance in a subsequent taxation year, the repayment increases the subsection 37(1) deductible pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and generates an ITC under subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8) calculated using the ITC rate from the year the assistance originally reduced the pool5. However, because repayments are not qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(9), the resulting ITC is strictly non-refundable in the year of repayment (it can only reduce Part I tax payable, carry back 3 years, or carry forward 20 years)5.

Non-Arm’s Length Allocation of Assistance (Form T1145): Where assistance is allocated among non-arm’s length parties, the parties must file prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm’s Length) under subsection 127(20) on or before the transferor’s filing-due date23.

body.text: 7.3 Worked Mathematical Optimisation: Stacking NRC IRAP with SR&ED Under the 55% Proxy Method

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 on the eligible SR&ED salary base before the NRC IRAP grant is deducted as government assistance in Part 4 (Line 515)22. Because NRC IRAP reimburses direct salary costs but does not cover employee overhead, the unreduced 55% PPA remains in the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool102.

Consider an Ontario CCPC in its 2026 taxation year that pays $100,000 in directly engaged T4 salary to a software engineer working 100% on an eligible SR&ED project, and receives an NRC IRAP grant of $40,000 (or $60,000) to subsidise that engineer’s salary22. In the $40,000 IRAP grant case (or $60,000 IRAP grant case shown in parentheses):

items: Direct Cash Outlay and IRAP Reimbursement: The company pays $100,000 in T4 SR&ED salary and receives +$40,000 (or +$60,000) in NRC IRAP grant funding, declared on Line 431 and Line 515 of Form T66122.

Gross SR&ED Qualified Expenditures Before Assistance (Form T661 Part 4 & Part 5): Directly engaged T4 salary on Line 300 is $100,000, and the 55% PPA on Line 820 / Line 502 is $55,000 (55% × $100,000), yielding $155,000 in gross qualified expenditures before assistance20.

Net Qualified Expenditures After Subtracting the IRAP Grant (Line 515): Subtracting the $40,000 IRAP grant from the $155,000 gross pool leaves $115,000 in net qualified expenditures (or subtracting a $60,000 IRAP grant leaves $95,000)22.
Ontario OITC (8% Refundable on Schedule 566): Multiplying $115,000 by 8% yields +$9,200 in refundable OITC (or on $95,000, +$7,600)78.
Ontario ORDTC (3.5% Non-Refundable on Schedule 508): Multiplying ($115,000 − $9,200 = $105,800) by 3.5% yields +$3,703 in non-refundable ORDTC (or on $95,000 − $7,600 = $87,400, +$3,059)78.

Federal SR&ED Enhanced ITC (35% Refundable on Schedule T2SCH31): Multiplying ($105,800 − $3,703 = $102,097) by 35% yields +$35,733.95 in refundable federal ITC (or on $87,400 − $3,059 = $84,341, +$29,519.35)78.
Total Combined Non-Dilutive Recovery on $100,000 Salary Outlay:
With a $40,000 IRAP Grant: $40,000 (IRAP) + $9,200 (OITC) + $3,703 (ORDTC) + $35,733.95 (Federal SR&ED) = $88,636.95 (88.64% of the $100,000 salary, with $84,933.95 in cash)22.
With a $60,000 IRAP Grant: $60,000 (IRAP) + $7,600 (OITC) + $3,059 (ORDTC) + $29,519.35 (Federal SR&ED) = $100,178.35 (or $98,190 in pure cash if the non-refundable ORDTC is waived)16.

body.text: Furthermore, because NRC IRAP can fund independent contractors or early feasibility/pre-commercial activities that are reduced (80% cap, no PPA) or excluded under SR&ED, strategically allocating NRC IRAP funds to cover contractor or non-SR&ED project tasks while reserving internal T4 experimental development salaries for unreduced SR&ED claims maximises total combined non-dilutive cash flow22.
